title: Binary, Bits & Flags
blurb: Count like a computer, mix colours in hex, and pack status effects and autotiles into single numbers with bitwise tricks.
intro:
Deep down, every number in a computer is a row of bits: tiny switches that are either 0 or 1. Most of the time you never think about them. But games use bits all the time: colours like #ff8800, collision layers, input buttons, status effects, and autotiling walls are all bit tricks.

In this section you'll learn to read binary and hex, then use the bitwise operators &, |, ^, ~, << and >> to pack lots of yes/no facts into one number.

Tip

Godot's collision layers and masks and GameMaker's colour functions both work exactly like the bit tricks here, so this knowledge travels with you between engines.
links: Godot Docs: Using TileSets (terrains and autotiling)

stages.l:
We count in decimal: each place is worth 10 times the one to its right (1, 10, 100...). Binary works the same way with 2: each place is worth double the one to its right.

8421Total
01014 + 1 = 5
10108 + 2 = 10
01114 + 2 + 1 = 7

To write a number in binary, pick the place values that add up to it. Each place is one bit.
stages.p: Work these out by hand and store each one as a string of 0s and 1s (no leading zeros): six, nine and fifteen.
stages.h: 6 is 4 + 2, so it's "110". 9 is 8 + 1. 15 is 8 + 4 + 2 + 1.

stages.l:
You don't have to do it by hand. n.toString(2) turns a number into a binary string. The 2 is the base.

(10).toString(2);    // "1010"
(7).toString(2);     // "111"

You can also write binary straight into your code with 0b: 0b1010 is just the number 10.
stages.p: Return n written in binary, as a string.
stages.h: Numbers have a toString method that takes a base. Base 2 is binary (base 16 would be hex).

stages.l:
Going the other way, parseInt(text, 2) reads a string as base 2.

parseInt("1010", 2);   // 10
parseInt("0111", 2);   // 7, leading zeros are fine
Tip

Always pass the base to parseInt. Without it, JavaScript assumes base 10.
stages.p: Return the number that the binary string bits stands for.
stages.h: parseInt takes a second argument: the base the string is written in. For example parseInt("ff", 16) is 255.

stages.l:
Binary gets long fast. Hexadecimal (base 16) is a shorter way to write the same bits. It uses the digits 0 to 9 then a to f for 10 to 15. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so two hex digits are one byte (0 to 255).

DecimalBinaryHex
101010a
151111f
25511111111ff
(255).toString(16);          // "ff"
(5).toString(16);            // "5"
"5".padStart(2, "0");        // "05"
0xff;                        // 255, hex written in code
stages.p: Return n (0 to 255) as a two-digit lowercase hex string, like "0a" for 10.
stages.h: n.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")

stages.l:
A colour like #ff8800 is three bytes in a row: red ff, green 88, blue 00. Each pair is a hex number from 0 to 255.

const hex = "#33cc99";
hex.slice(1, 3);                 // "33"
parseInt(hex.slice(1, 3), 16);   // 51
stages.p: Turn a colour like "#ff8800" into an array [r, g, b] of numbers.
stages.h: Red is parseInt(hex.slice(1, 3), 16), green is slice(3, 5), blue is slice(5, 7).

stages.l:
Bitwise operators work on each bit separately. & (AND) gives a 1 only where both numbers have a 1.

  1100   (12)
& 1010   (10)
= 1000   (8)

A common use: x & 1 looks at just the last bit. Odd numbers always end in a 1 in binary, even numbers in a 0.

Tip

Don't mix up & with &&. The double one is the logical "and" you use in if. The single one works on bits.
stages.p: Return true if n is odd, using & instead of %.
stages.h: The lowest bit of an odd number is 1. Use & with 1 to pick out that bit, then compare it.

stages.l:
Two more:

  • | (OR) gives a 1 where either number has a 1.
  • ^ (XOR, "exclusive or") gives a 1 where the bits are different.
  1100 | 1010 = 1110   (14)
  1100 ^ 1010 = 0110   (6)
stages.p: Return an array [a | b, a ^ b].
stages.h: Return an array with two entries: the OR of the two numbers (|) and the XOR (^).

stages.l:
~ (NOT) flips every bit: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0. JavaScript bitwise numbers have 32 bits, so ~5 flips all 32 and gives -6, which surprises everyone the first time.

To keep only the bits you care about, AND the result with a mask. 255 is 11111111, so & 255 keeps the lowest 8 bits.

~5;          // -6
~5 & 255;    // 250, which is 11111010
stages.p: Flip all 8 bits of the byte n and return a number from 0 to 255.
stages.h: ~ flips every bit, but also gives a negative number. Mask the result with & 255 to keep just the low 8 bits.

stages.l:
Shifts slide all the bits left or right.

  • x << n moves bits left by n places. Each step doubles the number.
  • x >> n moves bits right by n places. Bits that fall off the end are gone.
1 << 3;          // 8      0001 becomes 1000
0b1101 >> 2;     // 3      1101 becomes 0011

1 << n is a quick way to make a number with only bit n switched on. You'll use that a lot.
stages.p: A byte is two 4-bit halves called nibbles. Return [high, low]: the top 4 bits and the bottom 4 bits of n (0 to 255).
stages.h: The high nibble is n >> 4. The low one is n & 15 (15 is 1111).

stages.l:
Now the fun part. Think of a number as a row of on/off switches numbered from the right, starting at 0. To ask "is switch n on?", AND with a number that has only that bit on.

const flags = 0b0110;
(flags & (1 << 1)) !== 0;   // true, bit 1 is on
(flags & (1 << 0)) !== 0;   // false, bit 0 is off
stages.p: Return true if bit n of flags is on.
stages.h: Build a mask with only bit n on using 1 << n. AND it with flags and check whether the result is not zero.

stages.l:
To switch a bit on, OR it in. If it was already on, it stays on.

let flags = 0b0100;
flags = flags | (1 << 0);   // 0b0101
flags |= 1 << 0;            // still 0b0101, same thing, shorter
stages.p: Return flags with bit n switched on.
stages.h: Make a mask for bit n with 1 << n, then combine it with flags using OR.

stages.l:
To switch a bit off, AND with a mask that has every bit on except that one. ~ makes that mask for you.

~(1 << 1)              // ...11111101
0b0111 & ~(1 << 1);    // 0b0101
stages.p: Return flags with bit n switched off.
stages.h: Make a mask for bit n with 1 << n, invert it with ~, then AND it with flags.

stages.l:
XOR flips a bit: on becomes off, off becomes on. Perfect for things like a torch the player switches on and off.

let lights = 0b0000;
lights ^= 1 << 2;   // 0b0100
lights ^= 1 << 2;   // 0b0000 again
stages.p: Return flags with bit n flipped.
stages.h: Make a mask for bit n with 1 << n, then combine it with flags using XOR (^), which flips just that bit.

stages.l:
Here's why bits matter in games. Give each status effect its own bit, and one number can hold all of them:

const POISON = 1;   // 0001
const BURN   = 2;   // 0010
const FREEZE = 4;   // 0100
const STUN   = 8;   // 1000

let status = POISON | FREEZE;     // 0101, poisoned and frozen
if (status & FREEZE) console.log("Can't move!");
status &= ~POISON;                // cured the poison

Each constant is a power of two, so their bits never overlap. Checking status & FREEZE gives 0 (falsy) when the bit is off.
stages.p: Return an array of the names of every effect that is on in status, in the order POISON, BURN, FREEZE, STUN.
stages.h: Check each one: if (status & POISON) out.push("POISON"); and so on.

stages.l:
How many effects is a player suffering from? Count the 1 bits. One way: look at the last bit with & 1, then shift right, until nothing is left.

let flags = 0b1101, on = 0;
while (flags !== 0) {
  on += flags & 1;
  flags = flags >> 1;
}
// on is 3
stages.p: Return how many bits are on in n (a whole number, 0 or more).
stages.h: Use the same loop shape on n: keep a count, add the last bit each time, shift right, and return count at the end.

stages.l:
A power of two (1, 2, 4, 8...) has exactly one bit on. Here's a classic trick: subtracting 1 flips that bit off and turns on all the bits below it, so the two numbers share no bits.

  8 = 1000      6 = 0110
  7 = 0111      5 = 0101
8 & 7 = 0     6 & 5 = 0100  (not zero)

Texture sizes in old engines often had to be powers of two, so this check is a real one.
stages.p: Return true if n is a power of two. Remember that 0 is not.
stages.h: A power of two has exactly one bit on, so n & (n - 1) is zero for it. Also check that n is above zero, joining both tests with &&.

stages.reqMsg: Use << to move red and green into place.
stages.l:
Three bytes fit inside one number. Shift red up 16 bits, green up 8, and OR them together with blue:

  red   << 16   rrrrrrrr 00000000 00000000
  green << 8             gggggggg 00000000
  blue                            bbbbbbbb
  OR together   rrrrrrrr gggggggg bbbbbbbb

That's exactly how 0xff8800 is laid out. GameMaker stores colours as one number too (in blue, green, red order).
stages.p: Pack r, g and b (each 0 to 255) into a single number.
stages.h: Shift r left by 16 bits and g by 8 with <<, then glue all three together with |.

stages.l:
To get a byte back out, shift it down to the bottom and mask off everything above it with & 255.

const c = 0x123456;
(c >> 8) & 255;   // 0x34, which is 52
stages.p: Return [r, g, b] from a packed colour number.
stages.h: Red is (color >> 16) & 255, green is (color >> 8) & 255, blue is color & 255.

stages.l:
Ever wondered how a wall tile knows whether to draw an edge or a corner? Autotiling checks the four neighbours and builds a 4-bit mask:

NeighbourBitValue
up01
right12
down24
left38

Add up the values of the neighbours that are walls and you get a number from 0 to 15. A tileset with 16 wall pieces, in that order, gives you the right piece for every spot.

let mask = 0;
if (isWall(x, y - 1)) mask |= 1;   // up
if (isWall(x + 1, y)) mask |= 2;   // right
// ...
stages.p: grid is an array of strings where # is a wall. Return the mask for the tile at column x, row y. Anything outside the grid counts as not a wall.
stages.h: A safe helper: const wall = (cx, cy) => (grid[cy] || "")[cx] === "#"; Then check up (x, y - 1), right, down and left.

stages.l:
Time to build a real status-effect system. Every turn, a list of events changes the player's status, then the effects do their thing:

  • "add NAME" switches that effect on
  • "remove NAME" switches it off
  • "toggle NAME" flips it
  • "cure" clears everything

After the events: POISON deals 2 damage, BURN deals 3, and the player can only act if they're neither FROZEN nor STUNNED.

Tip

A lookup object turns a name into its bit: const BIT = { POISON: 1, BURN: 2, FREEZE: 4, STUN: 8 }; then BIT[name].
stages.p: Apply each event in events to status in order. Return { status, damage, canAct }.
stages.h: Split each event: const [action, name] = ev.split(" "); Use |=, &= ~ and ^= with BIT[name]. For canAct, check (status & (FREEZE | STUN)) === 0.
